chapter: Chemical Reactions and Equations (Class 10 Science, CBSE)
note: Mixed-form items with answers for concepts that already hold 40 MCQs: their 40 non-MCQ slots.

2725.stem: Define a reactant.
2725.answer: A reactant is a substance that is present at the start of a chemical reaction and is used up as the reaction proceeds.

2725.stem: Define a product.
2725.answer: A product is a new substance formed during a chemical reaction and written on the right of the arrow.

2725.stem: How does a catalyst differ from a reactant?
2725.answer: A catalyst speeds up the reaction but is recovered unchanged at the end, whereas a reactant is chemically consumed.

2725.stem: In 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, name the reactants.
2725.answer: Magnesium and oxygen, because both are written before the arrow.

2725.stem: Name the reactant in rusting that students most often forget.
2725.answer: Water. Iron does not rust in perfectly dry air, however much oxygen is present, so water is essential and is consumed into the rust.

2725.stem: What is a spectator ion?
2725.answer: A spectator ion is one that appears unchanged on both sides of an equation because it takes no part in the reaction itself.

2725.stem: Why can a substance that appears on both sides of an equation not be called a catalyst?
2725.answer: A catalyst must alter the rate of the reaction while remaining unchanged. A species that is simply present on both sides without affecting the rate is a spectator, not a catalyst.

2725.stem: What is meant by the limiting reactant, and why can an equation alone never identify it?
2725.answer: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first and so stops the reaction. An equation gives only the fixed ratios in which substances react; which one runs out depends on the amounts actually taken, which is experimental information.

2725.stem: Identify the reactants and products in each: (a) Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2, (b) CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2.
2725.answer: (a) Reactants: zinc and sulphuric acid. Products: zinc sulphate and hydrogen. (b) Reactant: calcium carbonate. Products: calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. In each case everything before the arrow is a reactant and everything after it is a product.

2725.stem: Explain why the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants in a closed vessel.
2725.answer: A chemical reaction only rearranges atoms into new combinations; no atom is created or destroyed. In a closed vessel nothing can enter or leave, so every atom present at the start is still present at the end. The total mass therefore stays exactly the same, which is the law of conservation of mass.

2725.stem: In Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, explain the role of each of the four substances named.
2725.answer: Zinc is a reactant: it is the free metal consumed as it displaces copper. Copper sulphate is a reactant: it supplies the copper that is displaced. Zinc sulphate is a product: the zinc has taken the sulphate from the copper. Copper is a product: it is set free as the metal and deposits as a red-brown solid. The sulphate group itself passes across unchanged and so is a spectator.

2725.stem: A reaction in an open dish gains mass. Explain how this is possible without breaking the law of conservation of mass.
2725.answer: In an open dish the system can exchange matter with its surroundings. If the substance combines with a gas from the air, usually oxygen, then atoms that were not on the balance at the start become part of the product. The sample therefore gains mass while the total mass of matter in the world is unchanged. Rusting iron and burning magnesium both behave this way.

2725.stem: 10 g of a compound decomposes into 6 g of a solid residue and a gas. Find the mass of gas and explain your reasoning.
2725.answer: The mass of gas is 10 g minus 6 g, which is 4 g. The reasoning is the law of conservation of mass: the compound is the only reactant, so the masses of the solid residue and the gas together must add up to the mass of the compound. If the experiment were done in an open vessel the gas would escape and the balance would appear to lose 4 g.

2725.stem: Explain why a product cannot normally also be listed as a reactant in the same simple equation.
2725.answer: The two sides of an equation record the state of the system before and after the change. A substance on the left is being consumed and one on the right is being formed, so the same substance cannot be both unless it is genuinely unchanged. If it does appear on both sides unchanged it is a spectator and is cancelled when the equation is written in ionic form. Listing it as both without cancelling would suggest it is simultaneously used up and made, which describes nothing.

2725.stem: A student says any substance whose mass falls during a reaction must be a reactant. Assess this reasoning.
2725.answer: The reasoning is unsound. It is true that reactants are consumed, so their mass falls, which makes the claim look plausible. But a product can also leave the system, for example as a gas escaping from an open vessel, and then its mass on the balance falls too. A falling mass therefore shows only that matter has left that part of the system, not what chemical role it played. To identify a reactant one must show it was present at the start and chemically consumed.

2725.stem: Two experiments start with the same reactants but give different products. Explain how this is possible.
2725.answer: The products of a reaction are determined not only by what is present but by the conditions under which they meet. Changing the temperature, the concentration, the amount of one reactant or the catalyst used can favour one reaction pathway over another. Carbon burning in plenty of air gives carbon dioxide, while the same carbon in a limited supply of air gives carbon monoxide. So conditions are part of the chemical description, not merely practical detail.

2725.stem: Assertion (A): Reactants are consumed during a reaction. Reason (R): Reactants are written on the left of the arrow. Choose the correct option.
2725.explanation: Both statements are true, but being written on the left is a convention of notation, not the cause of being consumed.

options.text: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Where a substance is written does not cause it to be consumed.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Reactants are conventionally written on the left.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Reactants are genuinely consumed during a reaction.

2725.stem: Assertion (A): In a sealed flask the mass stays constant even when gas forms. Reason (R): Gases have no mass. Choose the correct option.
2725.explanation: The assertion is true but the reason is false: gases do have mass, and the reading stays constant because the gas cannot leave the flask.

options.text: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Gases certainly have mass, which is why an open vessel loses weight.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: The mass really does stay constant in a sealed flask.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Nothing can leave a sealed flask, so the mass cannot change.

2725.stem: Assertion (A): A catalyst is not written as a reactant. Reason (R): A catalyst is not consumed by the reaction. Choose the correct option.
2725.explanation: Both are true, and not being consumed is precisely why a catalyst is not placed on the reactant side.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Being consumed is exactly the test for a reactant.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: A catalyst is recovered unchanged at the end.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: A catalyst is written above the arrow, not on the left.

2725.stem: Assertion (A): Conservation of mass means the number of molecules is conserved. Reason (R): Atoms are neither created nor destroyed. Choose the correct option.
2725.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: atoms are conserved, molecules are not, since one molecule can split into several or several can combine into one.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Conserving atoms does not conserve the number of molecules.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Atoms genuinely are neither created nor destroyed.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O turns three molecules into two.

2725.stem: State whether true or false: products are the substances formed during a reaction.
2725.explanation: By definition the products are what the reaction forms.

options.text: True
False
options.why: Substances formed during a reaction are exactly what products are.

2725.stem: State whether true or false: a catalyst is used up during the reaction it speeds up.
2725.explanation: A catalyst is recovered unchanged; being consumed is the mark of a reactant.

options.text: False
True
options.why: A catalyst is regenerated and recovered unchanged at the end.

2725.stem: State whether true or false: in an open vessel the mass of a reacting system can only decrease.
2725.explanation: It can also increase, as when iron rusts by taking oxygen and water from the air.

options.text: False
True
options.why: An open system can gain matter as well as lose it; rusting iron gains mass.

2725.stem: State whether true or false: if a product weighs less than the reactants, the law of conservation of mass has been broken.
2725.explanation: Some reactant may not have reacted, or some product may have been lost in handling; the law itself is never broken.

options.text: False
True
options.why: Incomplete reaction or loss during handling explains a low yield without any law being broken.

2725.stem: Substances present at the start of a reaction and used up are called ___________.
2725.answer: reactants

2725.stem: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being consumed is a ___________.
2725.answer: catalyst

2725.stem: An ion that appears unchanged on both sides of an equation is called a ___________ ion.
2725.answer: spectator

2725.stem: The reactant that runs out first and stops the reaction is called the ___________ reactant.
2725.answer: limiting

2725.stem: Explain the terms reactant, product, catalyst and spectator, giving one example of each from reactions you have studied.
2725.answer: A reactant is a substance present at the start and consumed during the reaction; in Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 both zinc and hydrochloric acid are reactants. A product is a new substance formed; in the same reaction zinc chloride and hydrogen are the products. A catalyst is a substance that changes the rate of the reaction but is recovered unchanged at the end, so it is written above the arrow rather than on either side; iron in the manufacture of ammonia is an example. A spectator is a species present on both sides of an equation without taking part; in Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu the sulphate group simply changes partner and is a spectator. The four terms describe four different roles, and a substance's role is decided by what happens to it, not by where it happens to be written.

2725.stem: Describe an experiment to verify the law of conservation of mass, including the apparatus, the procedure, the expected result and two precautions.
2725.answer: Apparatus: a conical flask with a tight rubber stopper, a small ignition tube, a balance reading to at least 0.01 g, and solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulphate. Procedure: place about 20 cm3 of sodium sulphate solution in the flask. Put about 5 cm3 of barium chloride solution in the small ignition tube and lower it carefully into the flask without letting the two mix. Stopper the flask tightly and weigh the whole assembly. Now tilt the flask so the two solutions mix; a white precipitate of barium sulphate appears at once. Weigh the flask again without removing the stopper. Expected result: the two readings are identical within the accuracy of the balance, showing that the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants. Precautions: the stopper must be tight throughout so nothing can escape or enter, and the flask must not be opened between the two weighings. It also helps to choose a reaction that produces no gas, so that no pressure builds up inside the flask.

2725.stem: A student burns magnesium in an open crucible and finds the residue heavier than the ribbon. Explain the result fully and describe how you would prove your explanation.
2725.answer: The residue is heavier because the magnesium has combined with oxygen from the air to form magnesium oxide. The oxygen atoms were in the surrounding air and not on the balance when the ribbon was weighed, so they represent added mass. The law of conservation of mass is not broken: the mass gained by the sample equals the mass of oxygen taken from the air. To prove this, weigh a clean crucible with lid, add a weighed length of magnesium ribbon and weigh again. Heat strongly, lifting the lid only briefly and at intervals so that air can enter but the white smoke of magnesium oxide cannot escape. Continue until heating produces no further change in mass. The increase in mass should equal the mass of oxygen predicted from the balanced equation 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. As a check, repeat the heating in a sealed tube containing a limited amount of air; the total mass of the sealed tube stays constant, confirming that nothing has been created and that the gain in the open crucible came from the air.

2725.stem: Discuss why the law of conservation of mass was not discovered until careful closed-vessel experiments were made.
2725.answer: Most of the reactions people observed before that time were carried out in the open. Burning is the obvious example: wood burns away to a small heap of ash, and the mass on the balance falls dramatically. The gaseous products, carbon dioxide and water vapour, disperse into the air and were never weighed, so the evidence available pointed to matter being destroyed. Some open reactions point the other way: a metal heated in air gains mass, which looked equally puzzling. With both kinds of result available and no way to account for gases, no simple regularity could be seen. Lavoisier's contribution was methodological as much as theoretical: by carrying out reactions in sealed vessels and weighing the whole vessel before and after, he made sure that nothing entered or left. Under those conditions the mass was always unchanged, and the earlier results became explicable as losses or gains from the surroundings rather than as creation or destruction of matter. The episode shows that a law can be hidden not by lack of care but by an uncontrolled boundary around the system being studied.

2725.stem: 6 g of carbon reacts completely with 16 g of oxygen. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed.
2725.answer: By the law of conservation of mass, mass of product = total mass of reactants = 6 g + 16 g = 22 g. Since the carbon reacts completely and no other product is formed, all 22 g is carbon dioxide.

2725.stem: 16 g of methane burns completely to give 44 g of carbon dioxide and 36 g of water. Calculate the mass of oxygen used.
2725.answer: Total mass of products = 44 g + 36 g = 80 g. By conservation of mass this equals the total mass of reactants, which is the methane plus the oxygen. Mass of oxygen = 80 g - 16 g = 64 g.

2725.stem: 5 g of A and 7 g of B are reacted and only 10 g of product C is collected. Calculate the shortfall and give two possible explanations.
2725.answer: Expected mass of C if both reacted completely = 5 g + 7 g = 12 g. Mass collected = 10 g, so the shortfall is 2 g. Two possible explanations: first, the reaction may have been incomplete, so 2 g of unreacted A or B remains mixed in with the product or left behind in the vessel. Second, some product may have been lost during transfer, filtering or drying. In neither case is mass destroyed; the 2 g still exists somewhere. If a gas were among the products and the vessel were open, escaping gas would be a third explanation.

2725.stem: Match each term in Column I with its description in Column II. Column I: (a) reactant, (b) product, (c) catalyst, (d) spectator ion. Column II: (i) formed during the reaction, (ii) unchanged on both sides and not involved, (iii) consumed during the reaction, (iv) speeds the reaction and is recovered.
2725.answer: (a) - (iii) consumed during the reaction. (b) - (i) formed during the reaction. (c) - (iv) speeds the reaction and is recovered unchanged. (d) - (ii) unchanged on both sides and not involved in the change.

2725.stem: For Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, match each substance in Column I with its role in Column II. Column I: (a) Zn, (b) CuSO4, (c) ZnSO4, (d) Cu. Column II: (i) product, (ii) reactant.
2725.answer: (a) Zn - (ii) reactant, the metal consumed. (b) CuSO4 - (ii) reactant, the salt consumed. (c) ZnSO4 - (i) product, formed in solution. (d) Cu - (i) product, deposited as free metal.

2725.stem: Draw a labelled diagram of the sealed-flask apparatus used to verify conservation of mass, and state what is weighed.
2725.answer: Draw a conical flask containing sodium sulphate solution, with a small ignition tube of barium chloride solution suspended inside it from a thread, and a tight rubber stopper closing the flask. Label the conical flask, the sodium sulphate solution, the ignition tube, the barium chloride solution, the thread and the rubber stopper. Show the flask standing on the pan of a balance. What is weighed is the entire sealed assembly, flask, stopper, ignition tube and both solutions together, once before the solutions are mixed and again after mixing has produced the white precipitate. Both readings are the same, since nothing can enter or leave.

2725.stem: Draw a labelled diagram showing how you would collect and weigh the gas produced in a reaction, so that conservation of mass can be checked in a reaction that gives off a gas.
2725.answer: Draw a conical flask containing the reactants, closed with a stopper carrying a delivery tube. The delivery tube leads to a gas syringe, or to an inverted measuring cylinder full of water standing in a trough. Label the flask, the reactants, the stopper, the delivery tube, the gas syringe or cylinder, and the trough of water. Show the whole assembly standing on a balance. The key point to label is that the gas is captured rather than allowed to escape, so that its mass remains part of the system being weighed. If a gas syringe is used the whole apparatus can be weighed before and after, and the reading is unchanged. If the gas is collected over water, its volume can be measured and its mass calculated, and that mass added to the residue accounts exactly for the apparent loss from the flask.

2725.stem: Prove, using a reaction of your choice, that the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products.
2725.answer: Take the reaction between sodium sulphate solution and barium chloride solution, which forms a white precipitate of barium sulphate and leaves sodium chloride in solution: Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl. Place the sodium sulphate solution in a conical flask and suspend an ignition tube of barium chloride solution inside it, then stopper the flask tightly. Weigh the sealed assembly; let the reading be m1. Tilt the flask so that the two solutions mix, and observe the white precipitate forming. Weigh the sealed assembly again; let the reading be m2. Experiment shows m2 = m1 to within the accuracy of the balance. Since the flask was sealed throughout, no matter entered or left, so the contents after the reaction are made of exactly the same atoms as the contents before it. The difference m2 - m1 is therefore the change in the total mass of the chemical system, and it is zero. The total mass of the products, barium sulphate and sodium chloride, equals the total mass of the reactants, sodium sulphate and barium chloride. The proof depends on the seal: repeating the experiment with the stopper removed and a gas-producing reaction would show a fall in mass, which is a loss from the balance and not a loss of matter.

2726.stem: What is a chemical equation?
2726.answer: A chemical equation is a statement of a reaction written with the chemical formulae of the reactants and products instead of their names.

2726.stem: Write the chemical formula of calcium carbonate.
2726.answer: CaCO3

2726.stem: What does the number 2 in 2H2O mean?
2726.answer: It is a coefficient, meaning two molecules of water, and it multiplies every atom in the formula that follows it.

2726.stem: Why is the subscript in a formula never changed while balancing?
2726.answer: The subscripts define which substance the formula represents, so changing one turns it into a different compound and changes the chemistry described.

2726.stem: How many oxygen atoms are there in one formula unit of Al2(SO4)3?
2726.answer: Twelve. Each sulphate group has four oxygen atoms and there are three such groups, so 4 x 3 = 12.

2726.stem: Write the formula of calcium hydroxide and explain why brackets are needed.
2726.answer: Ca(OH)2. Calcium has a valency of two and hydroxide has a valency of one, so two hydroxide groups are needed. The brackets make the 2 apply to the whole OH group; without them the 2 would apply only to the hydrogen.

2726.stem: Why is knowing the diatomic elements essential when writing chemical equations?
2726.answer: Hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and the halogens exist as two-atom molecules when free. Writing them as single atoms gives the wrong atom count on that side of the equation, so the balancing and any calculation from it would be wrong.

2726.stem: Can balancing an equation reveal that one of its formulae is wrong? Justify.
2726.answer: Usually not. A wrong formula can often still be balanced successfully, so the error survives the check. Balancing tests only whether atoms are conserved, not whether the substances written are the ones that really react.

2726.stem: Explain the difference between a coefficient and a subscript, with an example of each.
2726.answer: A coefficient is a full-size number written in front of a formula and it multiplies every atom in that formula; in 3CaCO3 the 3 means three whole formula units. A subscript is a small number written after a symbol within a formula and it applies only to the symbol it follows; in CaCO3 the 3 means three oxygen atoms. Coefficients may be changed freely when balancing, because they only say how many units react. Subscripts must never be changed, because they define what the substance is.

2726.stem: State three advantages of writing an equation in formulae rather than in words.
2726.answer: First, formulae give the number of atoms of each element, so the equation can be balanced and mass can be checked. Second, because the atom counts are known, masses and amounts of reactants and products can be calculated from the equation. Third, formulae are unambiguous internationally, whereas common names differ from place to place. A word equation identifies the substances but supports none of this.

2726.stem: Convert the word equation 'zinc + hydrochloric acid -> zinc chloride + hydrogen' into a balanced chemical equation, showing your steps.
2726.answer: Step 1, write the formulae: Zn, HCl, ZnCl2 and H2. Zinc has a valency of two, so the chloride is ZnCl2, and hydrogen gas is diatomic. Step 2, the skeletal equation is Zn + HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. Step 3, count the atoms: chlorine is one on the left and two on the right, and hydrogen is one on the left and two on the right. Step 4, put a coefficient of 2 in front of HCl, giving Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. Step 5, check: zinc one each side, hydrogen two each side, chlorine two each side. The equation is balanced.

2726.stem: Write balanced chemical equations for: (a) the burning of magnesium, (b) the decomposition of water by electricity.
2726.answer: (a) 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Oxygen is diatomic, so two magnesium atoms are needed to use both oxygen atoms and two units of magnesium oxide are formed. (b) 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2, with electricity written above the arrow. Two water molecules give two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule, which is why the hydrogen collected in electrolysis is twice the volume of the oxygen.

2726.stem: Write the formulae of sodium sulphate, aluminium sulphate and ammonium chloride, explaining how you worked each one out.
2726.answer: Sodium sulphate: sodium has a valency of one and sulphate a valency of two, so two sodium atoms are needed, giving Na2SO4. Aluminium sulphate: aluminium has a valency of three and sulphate two, so the lowest common multiple is six, requiring two aluminium and three sulphate groups, giving Al2(SO4)3 with brackets so the 3 applies to the whole group. Ammonium chloride: ammonium has a valency of one and chloride one, so they combine one to one, giving NH4Cl with no brackets needed.

2726.stem: Explain why a chemical equation can be perfectly correct in its notation and still describe a reaction that never occurs.
2726.answer: Correct notation guarantees only internal consistency: that every formula represents a real substance and that the atoms balance on the two sides. Neither of those tests says anything about whether the change actually takes place. Whether a reaction occurs depends on the reactivity of the substances and on the energy involved, which are matters for experiment and for the reactivity series. For example, Cu + FeSO4 -> CuSO4 + Fe can be written with correct formulae and balanced perfectly, yet nothing happens when copper is placed in iron sulphate solution, because copper is less reactive than iron.

2726.stem: A student balances an equation by changing H2O to H2O2 and the atoms now match. Assess this method.
2726.answer: The method is invalid, and the deepest objection is not that the arithmetic fails but that it succeeds. The atom counts may well come out equal, so the equation looks correct. But H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance from water with different properties, so the balanced equation now describes a reaction that was never carried out. Balancing must be done with coefficients only, because a coefficient says how many units of a substance react while a subscript says what that substance is. An equation that is internally consistent about the wrong substances is more dangerous than one that is visibly unbalanced, because nothing signals the error.

2726.stem: Why can the same element carry different subscripts in different compounds?
2726.answer: The subscript records the ratio in which the atoms combine in that particular compound, and that ratio is fixed by the valencies of both elements involved. Many elements show more than one valency: iron forms both FeO, where it behaves with a valency of two, and Fe2O3, where it behaves with a valency of three. The subscript is therefore not a property of the element alone but of the combination, which is why it is decided by the compound and cannot be altered to suit a balancing problem.

2726.stem: Assertion (A): Chemical equations must be balanced. Reason (R): Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Choose the correct option.
2726.explanation: Both are true, and conservation of atoms is exactly why the counts must match on both sides.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Conservation of atoms is precisely the reason balancing is required.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Atoms genuinely are neither created nor destroyed.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: An unbalanced equation would imply atoms appeared or vanished.

2726.stem: Assertion (A): Subscripts may be changed to balance an equation. Reason (R): Balancing must make the atom counts equal. Choose the correct option.
2726.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: changing a subscript changes the substance, so only coefficients may be adjusted.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: The atom counts must match, but only coefficients may be used to make them match.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Balancing does genuinely require equal atom counts.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Changing a subscript replaces the substance with a different one.

2726.stem: Assertion (A): Free oxygen is written as O2 in equations. Reason (R): Oxygen exists as a diatomic molecule when free. Choose the correct option.
2726.explanation: Both are true, and oxygen being diatomic is precisely why it is written O2.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Being diatomic is exactly the reason for the formula O2.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Free oxygen genuinely exists as two-atom molecules.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: O2 is the standard way free oxygen is written.

2726.stem: Assertion (A): A balanced equation proves the reaction occurs. Reason (R): A balanced equation conserves atoms. Choose the correct option.
2726.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: conserving atoms shows only internal consistency, and an invented reaction can be balanced perfectly.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Conserving atoms says nothing about whether the change happens.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: A balanced equation does conserve atoms, so R is true.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Cu + FeSO4 -> CuSO4 + Fe balances but does not occur.

2726.stem: State whether true or false: in 2Na the 2 is a subscript.
2726.explanation: A number written in front of a symbol is a coefficient; a subscript is written after and below.

options.text: False
True
options.why: The number in front of a formula is a coefficient, meaning two separate atoms.

2726.stem: State whether true or false: O2 represents an element even though it is a molecule.
2726.explanation: It contains only one kind of atom, so it is an element; being a molecule does not make it a compound.

options.text: True
False
options.why: A compound must contain two or more different elements; O2 contains only oxygen.

2726.stem: State whether true or false: 3CaCO3 contains nine oxygen atoms.
2726.explanation: Each formula unit has three oxygen atoms and the coefficient 3 multiplies this, giving nine.

options.text: True
False
options.why: Three units of CaCO3, each with three oxygen atoms, give nine in total.

2726.stem: State whether true or false: two balanced equations for the same reaction differing only by a factor of two describe different reactions.
2726.explanation: Multiplying every coefficient preserves all the ratios, so the chemistry is identical; only the scale of description differs.

options.text: False
True
options.why: Uniform multiplication changes the scale, not the substances or their ratios.

2726.stem: A number written in front of a chemical formula is called a ___________.
2726.answer: coefficient

2726.stem: The chemical formula of quick lime is ___________.
2726.answer: CaO

2726.stem: Balance the equation: 2Mg + ___________ -> 2MgO.
2726.answer: O2

2726.stem: In the formula H2SO4 there are ___________ atoms altogether.
2726.answer: seven, being two hydrogen, one sulphur and four oxygen

2726.stem: Describe, step by step, how a sentence about a reaction is turned into a balanced chemical equation, illustrating each step with the burning of magnesium.
2726.answer: Step one is to identify the reactants and the products from the sentence and write a word equation: Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium oxide. Step two is to replace each name with the correct chemical formula, using the valencies of the elements. Magnesium is Mg, free oxygen is diatomic and so is O2, and magnesium oxide is MgO because both elements have a valency of two. This gives the skeletal equation Mg + O2 -> MgO. Step three is to count the atoms of each element on both sides. Magnesium is one and one, which balances, but oxygen is two on the left and one on the right, which does not. Step four is to balance using coefficients only. Putting 2 in front of MgO makes oxygen two on each side but magnesium one against two, so a 2 is also needed in front of Mg, giving 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Step five is to check every element again: magnesium two each side, oxygen two each side. Step six is to add physical states and any condition, giving 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s) on heating. Throughout, only the coefficients have been changed; no formula has been altered.

2726.stem: Write balanced chemical equations with state symbols for five reactions of your choice, and state the type of each.
2726.answer: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s): a combination reaction and also an oxidation. CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g) on heating: a thermal decomposition, which is endothermic. Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s): a displacement reaction, since iron is more reactive than copper, and also a redox reaction. Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq): a double displacement, and because an insoluble solid separates out it is also a precipitation reaction. NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l): a neutralisation, which is a kind of double displacement and is exothermic. In each case the state symbols show what would actually be observed: a solid product, a gas escaping, a deposit forming or everything remaining in solution.

2726.stem: Explain why writing equations in formulae makes the law of conservation of mass checkable, and show with an example what happens when an equation is left unbalanced.
2726.answer: A formula states how many atoms of each element a substance contains, so an equation written in formulae carries a countable number of atoms on each side. The law of conservation of mass says no atom is created or destroyed, so the counts must match, and matching them is exactly what balancing does. A word equation carries names only, so there is nothing to count and nothing to check. Consider H2 + O2 -> H2O. There are two oxygen atoms on the left and one on the right, so as written the equation says one oxygen atom has disappeared. If this equation were used to calculate masses it would give a product mass smaller than the reactant mass, which no experiment would ever confirm. Balancing it to 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O restores four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side, and the mass calculated for the water now matches the combined mass of the hydrogen and oxygen used. The balanced form is therefore not a tidier version of the same statement but a different and correct one, and the unbalanced form is a claim that mass has changed.

2726.stem: Evaluate the claim that a chemical equation is a complete description of a chemical reaction.
2726.answer: A balanced chemical equation with state symbols and conditions is a remarkably compact description. It names every reactant and product unambiguously through their formulae, gives the ratio in which they react, shows the direction of change, indicates what will be observed through the state symbols, and records what must be supplied through the conditions written above the arrow. From it one can calculate the masses that react and the masses formed. However, it is not complete. It says nothing about the rate at which the change occurs, which depends on temperature, surface area and concentration. It says nothing about the mechanism, that is, the sequence of steps by which the reactants become the products, which may involve intermediates that never appear in the equation. It does not indicate how far the reaction goes, since many reactions reach an equilibrium rather than going to completion, and a plain arrow hides this. It gives no information about the energy released or absorbed unless that is added separately. The fair conclusion is that a chemical equation completely describes the stoichiometry of a reaction, and that stoichiometry is only one of several things worth knowing about it.

2726.stem: Count the total number of atoms of each element in 2Ca(OH)2.
2726.answer: Each formula unit of Ca(OH)2 contains one calcium, two oxygen and two hydrogen atoms, which is five atoms. The coefficient 2 doubles all of these. So there are 2 calcium atoms, 4 oxygen atoms and 4 hydrogen atoms, making 10 atoms in total.

2726.stem: Balance Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2 and state the coefficient of every species.
2726.answer: Start with the largest compound, Fe3O4, which needs three iron atoms and four oxygen atoms. Four oxygen atoms require four water molecules, which bring eight hydrogen atoms, forming four hydrogen molecules. The balanced equation is 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2. Coefficients: Fe is 3, H2O is 4, Fe3O4 is 1 and H2 is 4. Check: iron 3 each side, oxygen 4 each side, hydrogen 8 each side.

2726.stem: Balance C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O, explaining the order in which you balanced each element and why.
2726.answer: Balance carbon first, because it appears in only one compound on each side. Three carbon atoms in C3H8 fix the coefficient of CO2 at 3. Balance hydrogen next, for the same reason: eight hydrogen atoms fix the coefficient of H2O at 4. Now count the oxygen on the right: 3 CO2 gives 6 oxygen atoms and 4 H2O gives 4, making 10 in total. Oxygen on the left is free and diatomic, so its coefficient is 10 divided by 2, which is 5. The balanced equation is C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O. Oxygen was left until last because it is the only species that is a free element, so changing its coefficient cannot disturb any other element's count; balancing it first would have forced repeated rework as the carbon and hydrogen were settled.

2726.stem: Match each formula in Column I with its name in Column II. Column I: (a) CaO, (b) CaCO3, (c) Ca(OH)2, (d) CO2. Column II: (i) calcium carbonate, (ii) carbon dioxide, (iii) calcium oxide, (iv) calcium hydroxide.
2726.answer: (a) CaO - (iii) calcium oxide, also called quick lime. (b) CaCO3 - (i) calcium carbonate, also called limestone. (c) Ca(OH)2 - (iv) calcium hydroxide, also called slaked lime. (d) CO2 - (ii) carbon dioxide.

2726.stem: Match each notation in Column I with its meaning in Column II. Column I: (a) the 2 in 2NaCl, (b) the 2 in H2O, (c) the (aq) in NaCl(aq), (d) the delta above the arrow. Column II: (i) two atoms within one molecule, (ii) heat must be supplied, (iii) dissolved in water, (iv) two separate formula units.
2726.answer: (a) - (iv) two separate formula units, since it is a coefficient. (b) - (i) two atoms within one molecule, since it is a subscript. (c) - (iii) dissolved in water, since (aq) means aqueous. (d) - (ii) heat must be supplied, since the delta is the symbol for heating.

2726.stem: Draw an annotated version of the equation 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s), labelling every part of the notation.
2726.answer: Write the equation large and draw a labelled arrow to each feature. Label the 2 in front of Mg as a coefficient, meaning two atoms of magnesium. Label the (s) after Mg as a state symbol meaning solid. Label the 2 in O2 as a subscript, meaning oxygen exists as a two-atom molecule when free. Label the (g) after O2 as a state symbol meaning gas. Label the arrow as meaning 'gives', pointing from reactants to products. Label the 2 in front of MgO as a coefficient, meaning two formula units of magnesium oxide. Label the (s) after MgO as a state symbol meaning solid. Add a note above the arrow reading 'heat' or a delta, since the magnesium must be ignited. Add a final annotation showing the atom count check: magnesium two on each side, oxygen two on each side.

2726.stem: Draw a flow chart showing the full route from a word equation to a balanced chemical equation with state symbols, and mark where each of the two common errors can enter.
2726.answer: Draw five boxes joined by downward arrows. Box 1: word equation, naming reactants and products. Box 2: replace names with formulae using valencies, giving the skeletal equation. Box 3: count atoms of each element on both sides. Box 4: balance using coefficients only, working from the largest compound and leaving free elements last. Box 5: add state symbols and conditions. Mark the first common error with a warning arrow beside box 2: assigning a wrong formula, for example writing NaCl2 for sodium chloride. Annotate that this error is dangerous because the equation can still be balanced afterwards, so the check in box 4 will not catch it. Mark the second common error with a warning arrow beside box 4: altering a subscript instead of adding a coefficient, for example changing H2O to H2O2 to make the oxygen count work. Annotate that this error also leaves the equation looking balanced while describing a different reaction. Add a final feedback arrow from box 5 back to box 2 labelled 'recheck formulae against valencies', since that is the only step that catches the first error.

2726.stem: Show that the equation H2 + O2 -> H2O cannot be balanced by altering subscripts without changing the chemistry, and give the correct balanced form.
2726.answer: As written, the equation has two hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on the left, and two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom on the right. One oxygen atom is unaccounted for. Suppose we try to balance by altering a subscript, writing H2 + O2 -> H2O2. Now hydrogen is two on each side and oxygen is two on each side, so the atom counts match and the equation appears balanced. But H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, not water: it is a different compound, with different properties, which decomposes readily and is not the product of burning hydrogen. The equation is now internally consistent about a reaction that was not the one described, so the subscript change has not balanced the original equation at all; it has replaced it. Since subscripts are fixed by the identity of the substances, the only quantities free to change are the coefficients. Putting 2 in front of H2O gives two oxygen atoms on the right, matching the left, but now four hydrogen atoms on the right against two on the left; putting 2 in front of H2 restores that. The balanced equation is 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, with four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side, and every formula still representing the substance it did at the start.
